name: SECURITY Hive
os_min: Windows 2000 (present in all NT-based Windows versions)
location: HKLM\SECURITY (file: %SystemRoot%\System32\config\SECURITY): not readable in place even by local Administrator; requires SYSTEM privileges
purpose: Stores the Local Security Authority's policy database: the effective local audit policy, LSA secrets (service-account passwords, autologon password, machine account secret), and cached domain-logon credentials used when a domain controller cannot be reached.
key_fields: Policy\Secrets\<name>: encrypted LSA secrets (service-account credentials, machine account secret, autologon password)
Policy\PolSecretEncryptionKey: LSA key material, combined with the SYSTEM hive's boot key to decrypt Secrets
Policy\PolAdtEv: binary-encoded effective audit policy that LSASS consumes
Cache\NL$1 through NL$10: DCC2/MSCache v2 cached domain-credential hashes (Windows Vista and later)
normal_baseline: Cache slots (NL$x) are populated only on domain-joined systems that log on while off-network; Policy\Secrets contains only entries tied to known, installed services or scheduled-task run-as accounts; the audit policy reflected in PolAdtEv matches the organization's GPO baseline.
anomalies: PolAdtEv reflects fewer audit categories enabled than the organization's GPO baseline defines. E.g. process-creation or logon auditing disabled locally shortly before other suspicious activity, blinding downstream logging.
New or unexpected entries under Policy\Secrets that aren't tied to any known installed service (possible credential staging/harvesting).
Cache entries present on a system that isn't supposed to be domain-joined.
A Cache slot's last-write time with no corresponding logon event in the Security event log.
anti_forensic_notes: The SECURITY hive has no SACL configured by default, so routine access to LSA Secrets (e.g. via Mimikatz lsadump::secrets) generates no Security event log entries unless an analyst has proactively set an audit SACL on the key beforehand (which then generates Event ID 4656/4663 on access). MSCache v2 (DCC2) hashes cannot be used in pass-the-hash attacks and only yield a plaintext password via offline cracking, so their mere presence indicates exposure risk rather than confirmed compromise.
